    Train Sim World 7 Is the Best-Looking TSW Ever Made, and the Hardest One to Run

    By Zachary Holmes09/09/2026Updated:09/11/2026No Comments13 Mins Read
    Game: Train Sim World 7 Developer: Dovetail Games Publisher: Dovetail Games – TSW Genre: Train Simulation Full Release: September 15, 2026 Platform: PC (Steam, Epic) Editions: Free · $49.99 · $79.99 · $129.99 Rating: ESRB Everyone Steam Deck: Playable Reviewed On: PC — Advance Access build
    📋 Reviewed From Advance Access Train Sim World 7 doesn’t fully release until September 15. Deluxe and Ultimate pre-purchasers got in five days early, and this assessment — along with every Steam review currently visible — comes from that Advance Access build.

    Dovetail have a launch patch window ahead of them, and several issues below are exactly the kind that get addressed in it. Treat this as a pre-launch verdict.
    🤖 AI Disclosure, Filed on Steam Dovetail state that they use ElevenLabs’ text-to-speech tool to generate some voice-over elements — specifically in training modules and platform/onboard train announcements. All scripts are written by Dovetail staff; ElevenLabs generates the audio.

    We flag every disclosure we find. This one is unusually specific — it names the vendor and the exact features affected, which is more than most studios offer.
    Simulation Trains Transportation Sandbox Automobile Sim Exploration 3D Immersive Sim First-Person Realistic Atmospheric Driving Family Friendly Historical Modern Relaxing Controller Level Editor Moddable Open World
    3Core Routes
    4Editions
    159DLC Items
    8Languages
    35GBInstall
    🚂 Know this first: there’s a completely free edition. The Free Starter Edition gives you the Training Center, five trains and the core rolling stock for nothing. Before you spend anything — and the top edition is $129.99 — install that and find out whether TSW7 runs properly on your machine. Performance is the single most reported problem here.
    ⚖️ The Year the Long-Time Critics Softened Train Sim World ships annually, and the community response has settled into a familiar groove: it’s the same game again. TSW7 is the entry where that’s noticeably breaking down.

    The quotes speak for themselves. “The only new Train Sim World edition I haven’t complained about.” “Dovetail finally did something good.” “The most decent out of their recent releases.” “The most smooth and enjoyable experience on a TSW game.” These are from people with years of TSW and Train Simulator Classic behind them.

    The reason is mostly one thing: the visual overhaul is real. A new lighting system, an “Epic” settings tier above Ultra, DirectX 12, DLSS 4.5 with DLAA, and FSR 4 with frame generation. One player said the Leeds branch genuinely looked like real life.

    And yet it sits at Mixed. Because the other half of the story hasn’t changed at all.
    Find your way on the rails
    “Dearly wish Dovetail would fix the issues that have been reported since oh, the late 1960s, but generally this was money well spent.” The affection and the exasperation, in one sentence.

    Train Sim World 7 is the latest annual entry from Dovetail Games, arriving with three new core routes, a substantial graphics overhaul and a handful of genuinely new features. It fully releases September 15, with Deluxe and Ultimate buyers already playing.

    Our verdict: Train Sim World 7 delivers authentic railway simulation that appeals to both casual players seeking zen-like relaxation and hardcore enthusiasts chasing mastery. It’s the best-looking and best-received TSW in years, and it’s still fighting the same optimisation problems the series has always had.

    The Three Routes Are a Strong Selection

    🌴 Florida Tri-Rail

    Miami and Fort Lauderdale. Tri-Rail BL36PH, F40PH and Rotem cars, plus CSX freight and the Dura-Max Rock Hopper.

    🐑 Airedale & Wharfedale

    Yorkshire, and a network rather than a line. Northern BR Class 331, LNER Azuma, Class 66 and the Rylstone quarry.

    🏰 Nürnberg – Würzburg

    Bavaria, long-distance and regional. DB BR 440, BR 442 and the BR 193 Vectron.

    🎓 Training Center

    Included even in the free edition, with five trains and the core rolling stock.

    🔀 The Network Route Is the Real Win Of the three, Airedale & Wharfedale is the one drawing the most praise, and for a structural reason worth understanding.

    Most TSW routes are A to B — one line, one direction, a finite set of services. Airedale & Wharfedale is a network: multiple branches, junctions and a far wider spread of services to pick from. One long-time player put it directly — “instead of boring A to B routes, we finally have a network route as a core route.”

    That matters enormously for longevity. The most common complaint about train sims is that driving the same stretch repeatedly gets dull, and a branching network is the structural answer to it.

    The German and US routes are well regarded too, with players who normally stick to UK content saying this year’s selection changed their minds. The one grumble: the Florida route stops at Boca Raton rather than covering the full Tri-Rail line.

    Performance Is Still the Problem

    📉 25 FPS on the Flagship Route If there’s one reason TSW7 is sitting at Mixed rather than Positive, it’s this. Optimisation complaints appear in nearly every review we read, including the glowing ones.

    The specifics: one player reported dropping as low as 25 FPS on Airedale & Wharfedale — the route everyone agrees is the best thing in the package. Others describe the core routes as “not optimised well at times and can be laggy.” One summarised it as “while it seems slightly better, the optimization is still poor.”

    And the bugs are their own category. One reviewer shrugged and called it “a DTG classic”, which tells you how normalised this has become for the audience.

    This is the tension at the heart of TSW7: the new lighting and Epic settings are the headline feature, and the hardware cost of running them is the headline complaint. DLSS 4.5 and FSR 4 help — several players credit DLSS specifically — but they’re mitigating a problem rather than removing it.

    The New Features, and Where They Wobble

    🆕 Freight Hauler, Live Weather and the AI Guard Three genuinely new additions, all well-liked in concept, all still settling:

    FREIGHT HAULER lets you marshal freight with no instructions or schedule — cars populate the route, each needing a home, and how you switch, shunt and haul them is up to you. Players who prefer freight to passengers are delighted it exists and immediately want it on every route.

    LIVE WEATHER pulls real-time, location-specific conditions into the game. Lovely idea. In practice, players report it changing far too abruptly — clear skies to thunder in about two seconds.

    THE AI GUARD can now open and close doors on guard-operated trains, which is a real realism gain for driver-guard operations. It also, per one player, “sometimes forgets to do their job.”

    SAFETY SYSTEMS ON BY DEFAULT is the quiet winner. AWS, PZB and the rest can now be enabled from the off, as they’d be when taking over a real train — or left alone if you’d rather relax. Long-time players singled this out approvingly.

    One specific, reproducible bug worth flagging because a player documented it properly. Freight Hauler’s pathfinding sometimes routes you the wrong way — it appears to pick the nearest track to the destination rather than respecting the correct direction of travel on parallel lines, and when it does, the signals never turn green.

    The workaround: click your train on the map, clear the course, manually plot a route that puts you on the correct track for your direction, then set a fresh course to where you actually wanted to go. Annoying, but it unsticks you.

    The Editions Need Explaining

    This is where TSW7 asks the most of buyers, and the pricing structure deserves laying out plainly.

    Edition Price What You Get
    Free Starter Free Training Center, 5 trains, core UK/US/German rolling stock. A genuine free entry point, not a demo.
    Standard $49.99 All three new routes, 12 trains, 2 wagons. This is the actual game.
    Deluxe $79.99 Standard plus 3 more trains — Northern BR Class 333, DB BR 412 ICE 4, Tri-Rail GP49H-3 — and five days’ early access.
    Ultimate $129.99 Deluxe plus 3 additional routes and 16 more trains, drawn from TSW Compatible back-catalogue content.

    Two things to understand. First, $30 buys you three locomotives going from Standard to Deluxe. Second, the Ultimate tier’s extra content is “TSW Compatible” — Dovetail’s own term for material released for previous entries, which they note may be unchanged from its original release and may not use all newer core features.

    There are also 159 DLC items already listed against the game. A player’s advice is worth repeating verbatim: buy anything above Standard on sale, and buy DLC on sale, citing one route add-on at around £33 at full price.

    Things to Know Going In

    📋 Setting Expectations • Full release September 15. Pre-purchase promotion (10% off all paid editions) ends the same day
    • Mixed on Steam across 98 reviews, all from Advance Access players
    • Free Starter Edition exists — use it as a performance test before spending
    • Modes beyond driving: Free Roam, Conductor Mode, Photo Mode, Route Hopping. Conductor Mode is repeatedly mentioned as a good change of pace
    • Creators Club offers Livery Designer, Formation Designer and Scenario Planner — a Dovetail Live sign-up is required
    • Minimum spec is remarkably low (GTX 750 Ti, 8 GB RAM), but given the performance reports, treat the recommended RTX 2060 tier as the realistic floor
    • Steam Deck: Playable, not Verified. Partial controller support only
    • Requires a third-party EULA, and the ESRB flags in-game purchases
    • Eight languages, with full voice audio in English, French and German. Add-on localisation varies
    • Distant scenery and passenger models are the weak spots — one player called the LOD work “a bit naff at times” and noted no real improvement to passengers

    The Good, The Bad, & The Ugly

    The Good The Bad The Ugly
    The Lighting Overhaul Is a Genuine LeapA new lighting system, an Epic tier above Ultra, DX12, DLSS 4.5 with DLAA and FSR 4 with frame generation. Players who’ve complained about every previous entry are calling this one a real step up, and one said the Leeds branch looked like real life. Live Weather Changes Too AbruptlyReal-time location-specific weather is a lovely idea, but players report clear skies turning to thunder in about two seconds. The feature needs smoothing, not scrapping. 25 FPS on the Best Route in the GameOptimisation complaints appear in nearly every review, including the positive ones. The flagship Airedale & Wharfedale network is where players report the worst drops — the new lighting is the headline feature and its cost is the headline complaint.
    Airedale & Wharfedale Is a Network, Not a LineMultiple branches and junctions rather than another A-to-B run, which directly answers the genre’s biggest longevity problem. Long-time UK players are noticeably pleased, and the German and US routes converted people who normally skip them. The AI Guard Forgets Its JobGuards opening and closing doors is a real realism gain for driver-guard operations — when it works. Players report it intermittently failing to do anything at all. Freight Hauler’s Pathfinding Sends You the Wrong WayIt appears to pick the nearest track to the destination rather than the correct direction of travel, and when it does the signals never clear. There’s a manual workaround, but it’s a shame on the game’s most interesting new mode.
    Safety Systems On By DefaultAWS, PZB and the rest can now be active from the moment you step into the cab, as they would be taking over a real train — or left off if you want a relaxing run. A small option that veterans specifically praised. Distant Scenery and Passengers Lag BehindLOD work described as “a bit naff at times,” and no meaningful improvement to passenger models. The cabs are extremely detailed; the middle distance and the people are where the budget clearly didn’t go. $129.99 at the Top, and 159 DLC ItemsThirty dollars separates Standard from Deluxe for three locomotives, and Ultimate’s extra content is back-catalogue “TSW Compatible” material that may not use newer features. Players advise buying anything above Standard on sale — one route add-on runs around £33 alone.
    A Free Edition That Isn’t a DemoThe Free Starter Edition ships the Training Center, five trains and core rolling stock for nothing — which doubles as the ideal way to test performance on your own machine before committing a penny. Still Buggy, and Everyone Expects ItOne reviewer called the bug count “a DTG classic” and moved on. That resignation is its own kind of criticism, and it’s been earned over several releases. The Annual Release Question Hasn’t Gone AwayEven positive reviewers are asking Dovetail to stop shipping yearly. TSW7 is the strongest argument yet that more time produces a better game — which is also an argument against the schedule that produced it.

    The Verdict

    Train Sim World 7 is the entry where Dovetail’s harshest long-term critics started conceding. That’s genuinely notable for a series whose annual cadence had turned its own community sceptical, and it’s earned: the lighting overhaul is a real leap, the sound design is meaningfully better, the route selection is the strongest in years, and Airedale & Wharfedale being a branching network rather than another straight line is exactly the structural change the format needed.

    The new features are good ideas at varying stages of completion. Freight Hauler is the most exciting thing here and players immediately want it everywhere — but its pathfinding will occasionally strand you. Live weather is charming and far too abrupt. The AI guard is a realism win that sometimes forgets to show up.

    And then there’s the thing that’s always there. Performance remains the series’ unsolved problem, and this year it’s sharpened by the fact that the best-looking TSW ever made is also the one asking most of your hardware. Dropping to 25 FPS on the route everyone agrees is the highlight is a hard thing to look past, and it’s why this sits at Mixed while individual reviews read like recommendations.

    The honest read: install the Free Starter Edition first. It costs nothing, it uses the same engine, and it will tell you in twenty minutes whether TSW7 runs acceptably on your machine — which is the only question that actually matters here. If it does, Standard at $49.99 is the edition to buy; the jump to Deluxe is thirty dollars for three locomotives, and Ultimate is largely repackaged back catalogue. Wait for a sale on anything above Standard, and wait for a sale on DLC full stop.

    This is a pre-launch verdict, and Dovetail have a patch window before the 15th. If the optimisation pass lands, this becomes an easy recommendation. If it doesn’t, TSW7 will be remembered as the best TSW nobody could run properly — which would be a genuine shame, because the rest of it is the best work they’ve done in years.
